title: Chapter XXXI
summary: Jane begins teaching twenty poor girls at Morton. She honestly recognizes her first recoil from poverty and ignorance, then corrects it by affirming her pupils' equal human potential. Her clean cottage, work, and honesty prove preferable to luxurious dependence as Rochester's mistress, though she still grieves for him. St. John urges disciplined forward motion and explains his missionary calling as a conquest over his nature. Rosamond Oliver arrives, and Jane sees that St. John passionately loves the beautiful heiress while deliberately refusing her.
events: Jane opens the village school and commits herself to developing her pupils' capacities despite initial class prejudice.
She reaffirms that free, honest work is better than enslaving pleasure with Rochester.
St. John describes redirecting worldly ambition into missionary purpose.
Rosamond Oliver's visit exposes powerful mutual attraction that St. John sternly suppresses.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.development: Converts abstract equality into daily work among poor pupils and confirms her choice of freedom despite grief.

characters.name: St. John Rivers
characters.development: Reveals that his self-mastery can become despotic self-denial, treating human love as an obstacle to vocation.

characters.name: Rosamond Oliver
characters.development: Introduced as warm, beautiful, wealthy, and openly drawn to St. John.

threads.text: Jane builds an independent life without ceasing to love or worry about Rochester.
St. John sacrifices possible happiness with Rosamond to his missionary design.
